pages.text: The Moon is 384,400 kilometres from Earth on average. That sounds enormous. In cosmic terms, it is next door. The Sun is 150 million kilometres away. The nearest star beyond the Sun is more than 40 trillion kilometres distant. The Moon is the only body beyond Earth that humans have ever visited. On the night of 20 July 1969, Neil Armstrong stepped onto the lunar surface and became the first human being to stand on another world.

image.note: Illustration of the Moon's surface with Earth visible in the black sky above the lunar horizon

pages.text: The Moon formed approximately 4.5 billion years ago, shortly after the formation of the Earth. The most widely accepted theory is that a Mars-sized object, which scientists call Theia, collided with the early Earth. The impact was so violent that it blasted an enormous amount of material into orbit around Earth. Over time, this material coalesced to form the Moon.

The Moon is the fifth largest moon in the solar system and the largest relative to the size of its parent planet. Its diameter is about a quarter of Earth's. It has no atmosphere, no weather, and no magnetic field. Without an atmosphere to burn them up, meteorites strike the surface directly, creating the craters that cover it. The largest craters are visible from Earth with the naked eye on a clear night.

The Moon controls more than the tides. Its steady gravitational hand holds the earth's tilt stable, and it is that tilt which gives us reliable seasons and, ultimately, a climate calm enough for civilisation. The Moon is also drifting away, about four centimetres a year, slowing the earth's spin as it goes. Long ago, an earth day lasted only a handful of hours. The Moon has been lengthening our days, quietly, for billions of years.

The Moon's gravitational pull on the Earth creates the tides. As the Moon orbits the Earth, its gravity pulls the ocean toward it, creating a bulge of water on the side of the Earth facing the Moon and a corresponding bulge on the opposite side. As the Earth rotates beneath these bulges, coastal areas experience the rising and falling of sea level that we call the tide. In most places, there are two high tides and two low tides every day.

pages.text: The Moon also stabilises the Earth's axial tilt. The Earth rotates on an axis tilted at about 23.5 degrees from vertical. This tilt is what produces the seasons. Without the Moon's gravitational stabilising effect, the Earth's axial tilt would vary chaotically over time, producing extreme and unpredictable climate swings that would make conditions on the surface far less stable for life.

The Moon rotates at exactly the rate needed to keep one face permanently toward the Earth. This is not a coincidence. It is the result of tidal locking, a process in which the Earth's gravity has gradually slowed the Moon's rotation until it exactly matches its orbital period. The far side of the Moon, which was hidden from human eyes until the Soviet Luna 3 spacecraft photographed it in 1959, is rockier and more cratered than the near side.

The Moon has no weather, so it forgets nothing. With no wind or rain to erase them, the footprints left by the Apollo astronauts will remain crisp for millions of years. Every crater is a preserved record of an ancient impact. By counting craters, scientists can read the age of a lunar surface like rings in a tree. The Moon is a museum with no cleaners, holding the solar system's violent history exactly as it happened.

A total lunar eclipse turns the Moon deep red, and the reason is beautiful. When the earth passes directly between sun and Moon, it blocks the direct light, but the earth's atmosphere bends and filters some sunlight around the edges, letting only red wavelengths through. That red light falls on the Moon. In effect, the blood Moon glows with the combined light of every sunrise and sunset happening on earth at that moment.

Between 1969 and 1972, twelve human beings walked on the Moon. All were American astronauts. All were men. The programme that put them there, Apollo, was the largest and most complex peacetime engineering project ever undertaken. At its peak, it employed more than 400,000 people.

The Apollo missions brought back 382 kilograms of lunar rock and soil samples, which have been studied by scientists ever since and continue to yield new information about the formation of the Moon and the early solar system. They placed seismometers on the surface that detected moonquakes. They left retroreflectors, mirrors that allow scientists on Earth to measure the distance to the Moon precisely using laser pulses.

pages.text: No human has been to the Moon since December 1972, when the crew of Apollo 17 departed the surface. Fifty years later, NASA's Artemis programme aims to return, with the stated intention of landing the first woman and the first person of colour on the Moon. Other countries, including China, India, and several commercial organisations, have active lunar programmes.

India's Chandrayaan-3 mission landed near the lunar south pole in 2023, making India only the fourth country to achieve a soft landing on the Moon and the first to land near the poles. The south pole is of particular interest because permanently shadowed craters there may contain water ice, which would be a vital resource for any future permanent human presence on the Moon.

The race to the Moon was as much about fear as wonder. In the Cold War, the United States and the Soviet Union competed to prove which system could reach it first. The Soviets led early, with the first satellite, the first man in space, and the first images of the Moon's hidden far side. The Americans answered with Apollo. Rivalry funded the greatest expedition in history. Whatever drove it, twelve human beings walked on another world.

Every culture on earth has myths, stories, and beliefs centred on the Moon. In many African traditions, the Moon is female and the Sun male. In Igbo tradition, Onwa is the moon deity. The Yoruba word for month, osu, is the same as the word for Moon, reflecting how deeply the lunar cycle is embedded in Yoruba understanding of time. The Hausa lunar calendar, like the Islamic lunar calendar it draws from, uses the appearance of the new crescent moon to mark the beginning of months and to determine the timing of festivals including Ramadan and Eid.

The Islamic lunar calendar, which governs the timing of religious observances for Nigeria's large Muslim population, is entirely based on the Moon's cycle. The month begins with the sighting of the crescent moon. The month of Ramadan moves through the solar year because the lunar year is approximately eleven days shorter than the solar year. This means Ramadan falls at different times of the solar year over a cycle of approximately 33 years.

The Moon that hangs over Abuja on a clear night is the same Moon that hangs over every other city on earth. It is close enough to see detail with binoculars: the grey plains called mares, the bright crater rims, the shadows that shift with the angle of sunlight. It is the most accessible astronomical object in the sky and the most human.

pages.text: Now the Moon beckons again, and Africa is part of it. New missions from many nations aim to build lasting bases near the lunar south pole, where shadowed craters may hold water ice to drink, breathe, and turn into rocket fuel. African space agencies, Nigeria's among them, are joining international lunar science. The children reading this may live to see a permanent human outpost on the Moon, and some may help to build it.
